title: Stomach illness in a group
summary: Treat the sick person with the Emergency protocols, and protect everyone else: keep them apart with one carer and their own toilet, keep them away from food and water, wash hands with soap, and check the water.
doFirst: Care for the sick person with the Severe vomiting or diarrhea and Dehydration protocols.
Keep them apart from the others, with their own toilet or bucket and one carer.
They prepare no food and handle no water for others until 3 days after their symptoms stop.
Everyone washes hands with soap and water. Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.
Check that every drop the group drinks is being treated.

blocks.p: This topic is about protecting the rest of the group. For the sick person’s care, what to drink and the danger signs that mean they need medical help, use the protocols.

list: Diarrhea spreads through contaminated food or drinking water, or from person to person through poor hygiene (WHO).
Water with human feces in it, from sewage, septic tanks and latrines, is a particular danger (WHO). Food is another major cause when it is prepared or stored in dirty conditions (WHO).
Norovirus, a common cause of vomiting and diarrhea, is in vomit and poop, can be there before symptoms start, and can stay in poop for 2 weeks or more after the person feels better (CDC).
It can stay on surfaces for up to two weeks (University of Minnesota Extension).

blocks.p: When two or more people get the same illness from the same food or drink, CDC calls it a foodborne outbreak. Check the shared things first:

list: Water: is every drop that people drink, cook with and brush teeth with being boiled or treated (CDC)? Recheck how it is done, the dose and the waiting time (Make water safe). Recheck the source too.
Food: what did everyone eat? Throw away food that might be contaminated: norovirus can be in food that looks, smells and tastes normal (CDC).
Who cooked: was anyone preparing food while ill, or just after? (Minnesota Department of Health investigators ask this.)

blocks.p: Several people ill at the same time can also mean a shared poison or fumes from a stove, heater or engine: the Severe vomiting or diarrhea protocol checks for these.

list: Put them in a separate room or part of the shelter or camp, away from people who are not sick (CDC, evacuation centers), as far as your space allows.
Several sick people can share one area, but keep beds or cots at least 3 feet (90 cm) apart (CDC, evacuation centers).
Give them their own toilet or bucket toilet that only sick people use (CDC, Minnesota Department of Health). See Toilets when the water is off.
Serve their food away from people who are not sick, if you can (CDC).

Keep them apart until 3 days (72 hours) after their vomiting and diarrhea stop (Minnesota Department of Health). CDC’s evacuation-center guidance says at least 24 hours; this app uses the longer time.

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

list: CDC asks that a sick child be looked after by only one adult, the same one until 24 hours after symptoms stop. Do the same for any sick person if you can, so fewer people are exposed.
The carer washes hands with soap and water before and after caring for the sick person (CDC), and wears gloves to clean up vomit or diarrhea and to handle soiled laundry (CDC).
Someone who is ill does not care for others (CDC).

blocks.warn: Anyone who has had vomiting or diarrhea must not prepare or handle food, or handle the group’s water, until 3 days (72 hours) after their symptoms stop (Minnesota Department of Health; University of Minnesota Extension). CDC says: “Wait at least 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.” This app uses the longer time.

list: Cooks wash with soap and water before they start; hand sanitizer does not replace it for them (CDC).
Don’t touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands; use utensils (University of Minnesota Extension).
Wash fruit and vegetables carefully before you prepare them (CDC).
Wash dishes and food surfaces, then sanitize them with bleach (see Clean and disinfect).
Everyone washes with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after the toilet and before eating or handling food (CDC).
Use soap and water, not sanitizer: hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus and is not a substitute for handwashing (CDC).
Put a hand-washing station by the sick person’s toilet and one where food is made (Oregon State University Extension).

Clean up vomit or diarrhea straight away (Minnesota Department of Health): gloves, soak it up, bag it, wash with soap and water, then disinfect with the strong bleach mix and leave it wet (CDC). The full steps and the mix are in Clean and disinfect.
Wash soiled clothes and bedding at once, with gloves, without shaking them (CDC).

Clean door handles and other things the sick person touches often, with the surface mix. Use the strong vomit and diarrhea mix on their toilet seat or bucket and on anything soiled with vomit or diarrhea (CDC).

sections.h: How long to keep it up

blocks.p: Keep the separate toilet, the food rule and strict hand washing going until 3 days after the last person’s symptoms stop (Minnesota Department of Health). Norovirus can stay in poop for 2 weeks or more after someone feels better (CDC), so keep washing hands with soap after the toilet.

sections.h: When it is beyond the group

blocks.p: The protocols list the danger signs that mean someone needs medical help. Go through them for each sick person, and recheck them.
